impact_summary: On January 31st, GitLab.com experienced a severe database incident that began with a load spike (suspected spam) and escalated after replication failed and about 300 GB of production PostgreSQL data was accidentally deleted. Database data created between January 31st 17:20 UTC and 23:30 UTC was lost, including an estimated 5000 projects, 5000 comments, and roughly 700 users, affecting only GitLab.com users. Recovery required restoring from a six-hour-old LVM snapshot, with GitLab.com restored on February 1st around 18:00 UTC, roughly 18 hours of copying alone.

action_items.action: Enable WAL archiving for the production PostgreSQL cluster so replicas can catch up from archived segments instead of requiring manual re-synchronisation.
Enable automated Azure disk snapshots and regular verified pg_dump/base backups for all database servers, with restore tests run on a schedule.
Fix the backup procedure to use the pg_dump binary matching the production PostgreSQL major version, and fail loudly when versions mismatch.
Add monitoring and alerting that verifies a successful backup has completed within the expected window and pages on absence, rather than relying on cronjob emails.
Enable DMARC for the email domain used by cronjob and system notifications so failure alerts are delivered.
Add safeguards to destructive database operations, such as hostname/role checks and an explicit confirmation step that verifies the target is the secondary before wiping a data directory.
Review and correct the max_connections setting and document a standard configuration review process for PostgreSQL parameters.
Document pg_basebackup's silent waiting behaviour in the engineering runbooks and create a tested, step-by-step replica rebuild runbook.
Set up a disaster-recovery runbook and conduct regular restore drills so recovery paths are verified before they are needed, rather than relying on ad hoc Slack coordination.
Scale out database load by evaluating read replicas or query load balancing, reducing the single primary as a single point of failure.
Fix the account-removal background job so flagged accounts are not scheduled for hard deletion, and add rate limits to bulk deletion jobs.
Restrict ad hoc out-of-schedule production snapshots and require a documented change request for any production data copy to staging.
Upgrade staging database storage to premium disks or otherwise ensure restore throughput is sufficient to meet recovery time objectives.
